# The house sparrow in the service of basic and applied biology ## Authors - Haley E Hanson1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-0513-5911](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0513-5911)) † - Noreen S Mathews1 - Mark E Hauber2 - Lynn B Martin1 ### Affiliations 1. Global and Planetary Health, University of South Florida Tampa United States 2. Department of Evolution, Ecology, and Behavior University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign Urbana United States † Corresponding author ## Abstract From the northernmost tip of Scandinavia to the southernmost corner of Patagonia, and across six continents, house sparrows (Passer domesticus) inhabit most human-modified habitats of the globe. With over 7,000 articles published, the species has become a workhorse for not only the study of self-urbanized wildlife, but also for understanding life history and body size evolution, sexual selection and many other biological phenomena. Traditionally, house sparrows were studied for their adaptations to local biotic and climatic conditions, but more recently, the species has come to serve as a focus for studies seeking to reveal the genomic, epigenetic and physiological underpinnings of success among invasive vertebrate species. Here, we review the natural history of house sparrows, highlight what the study of these birds has meant to bioscience generally, and describe the many resources available for future work on this species. ## Introduction House sparrows are small, sexually dimorphic birds in the family Passeridae. The species is one of the most widely distributed and common birds in the world, represented by 12 different subspecies (Summers-Smith, 2009). House sparrows can be found living and breeding in climactically extreme environments from deserts in southern California to cities above the Arctic circle, where they are found almost exclusively in close proximity to human habitation (Hanson et al., 2020b). Considered anthrodependent, some populations have gone extinct locally without human presence (Ravinet et al., 2018; Summers-Smith, 1988). It is for this relationship with people that they received their species identifier domesticus, which derives from the Latin domus or 'house', from Carl Linnaeus in 1758 (Jobling, 2009; Anderson, 2006). Their ubiquity and close association with humans have undoubtedly led to their detailed study across biological and even sociological disciplines. Here, we explore the natural history of house sparrows and the contributions that these birds have made to basic biology and beyond. ## Native distribution and natural range expansions House sparrows are native to parts of Asia, North Africa and most of Europe, (with the exception of Italy which is occupied by the Italian sparrow P. italiae; Animation 1). Becoming commensal some 10,000 years ago, house sparrows are now strongly associated with habitats that have been modified by humans. However, they also continue to increase their geographic range by exploiting ongoing and accelerating anthropogenic change (Ravinet et al., 2018; Saetre et al., 2012). A reliance on humans is evident from their colonization of Northern Europe, Eastern Europe and Central Asia in the early 1800s, as agriculture spread and urbanization increased (Summers-Smith, 1963). Though still widespread, significant declines have been reported in the native range of the species since the 1970s. This topic remains contentious (Box 1), but these declines have been attributed to a multitude of factors, including infectious disease, pollution, pesticide use, predator dynamics, new building methodologies and more efficient grain harvesting and storage (Shaw et al., 2008; Summers-Smith, 2003; Singh et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2010; Dadam et al., 2019). ![Animation 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/52803/elife-52803-video1.gif.jpg) ## Introduced distribution and range expansions House sparrows are one of the most ubiquitous birds in the world (Anderson, 2006). In approximately 170 years, they colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica and occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2 (Birdlife international, 2018). There have been over 250 introduction or translocation events recorded worldwide (Table 1), with the first deliberate successful introduction occurring in 1851 in New York City (Summers-Smith, 1988). Many introductions stemmed from colonial acclimatization societies purposefully releasing birds for cultural reasons or as failed attempts at biological control. More recently, introductions have been accidental. Ship-assisted dispersal (e.g., cargo ships, cruise liners) has been documented, and other types of vehicle-assisted dispersal are also likely (Sainz‐Borgo et al., 2016; Schrey et al., 2014; Clergeau et al., 2004; Szent-Ivány, 1959; Summers-Smith, 1963). **Table 1.** Global house sparrow introduction or translocation events by region.Introduction and translocation events include both purposeful and inadvertent release of any number of birds from all subspecies, successful or unsuccessful. ## Dimorphism in morphology and behavior Male house sparrows tend to be heavier and larger than females (Figure 1; Hanson et al., 2020b). Plumage coloration differs between the sexes. Males have gray crests and black post-ocular stripes with conspicuous white spots behind the eyes (Figure 1b). Male abdomens are gray whereas bills, tails, wings and body feathers are black or dark brown. Plumage in females is drabber, with crests that are dark brown and post-ocular stripes that are light brown. Females lack black head markings and have gray-brown to light brown cheeks, bills and feathers (Figure 1a). Female plumage resembles juveniles and females from other Passer species so much that distinguishing them visually is often difficult (Anderson, 2006). Subspecies also differ in size, mass and male plumage (See Summers-Smith, 1988). ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/52803/elife-52803-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) Female house sparrow. (B) Male house sparrow. (C) Nestling house sparrows. (D) Male house sparrow provisioning nestlings. Image Credits: All images taken by Janneke Case in Tampa, Florida, United States, in 2019. The most conspicuous morphological difference between male and female sparrows is the large black throat badge of males. Arguably, this badge is one of the factors that made this species a model in behavioral ecology (Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018). Large badge size has been thought to convey an individual’s propensity to win in male-male competitive interactions; the logic was that possessing information a priori about a competitor could save both the badge-holder and his opponents from wasted energy and risk of injury (Rohwer, 1975). Recently, however, the largest meta-analysis to date revealed that badge size is at best an unreliable signal of dominance status (Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018). The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996). Importantly, many morphological characteristics also vary geographically. Most well-known through the pioneering work of Richard F Johnston and Robert K Selander, plumage color and aspects of body size (wing, tail and tarsus length, skeletal characteristics, and body mass) were found to vary within and between native and introduced populations (Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1964; Johnston and Selander, 1971; Johnston, 1969; Johnston, 1973). Introduced populations in North America were discovered to have pale coloration in hot, arid climates, but darker coloration in cooler, humid climates (Johnston and Selander, 1964). Body size of birds also increased with latitude, and perhaps most interestingly, all of these geographic trends in biological traits arose rapidly in the introduced populations (Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971). ## Diet and foraging Nestling house sparrows are fed an insect-based diet for the first three days after hatching. Later, following fledging, they favor grains, especially outside urban areas (Anderson, 2006). Adult house sparrows have a fairly opportunistic diet throughout much of the year, especially in cities and suburbs where human refuse is plentiful (Summers-Smith, 1988). One of the reasons house sparrows are so adept at exploiting diverse diets might involve plasticity in the release of digestive enzymes (Brzek et al., 2009). Behaviorally, responses to food also seem to play a role in range expansions, another reason this species has been used as a model. For example, house sparrows in the roughly 40-year-old Panama population consume unfamiliar foods more quickly than birds from a much older invasive population in New Jersey in the United States (Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005). A similar pattern is observed among Kenyan sparrows such that birds living at the expanding range edge of that colonization approach and eat novel foods more quickly than birds from the core of the population (Liebl and Martin, 2014). A tendency to eat novel foods may benefit birds in habitats where resources are scarce or unfamiliar, but such behavior could also come with risks. Spoiled foods or exposure to novel toxins, for example, may activate the immune system (Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005). This notion is supported by the observation that populations differ quite extensively in how their immune systems are organized and what parasites they harbor throughout their lives (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2014; Coon and Martin, 2014; Coon et al., 2014). ## Breeding biology Sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities, but they also routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures (Figure 1c) as well as in densely branched trees and shrubs (Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017). Nests are comprised mostly of vegetation but some clay, sand, cloth and even dung may be used (Heij, 1986). In some cities, nests also contain aromatic plants or even cigarette butts that contain antiparasitic secondary compounds (Sengupta and Shrilata, 1997). Males initially choose nesting sites and subsequently advertise for mates by vocal and visual displays (Summers-Smith, 1963). However, unlike many songbirds, males exhibit aggressive, territorial behavior only in a very small area around the nest site. Females select males based on visual and vocal displays and the location of nest sites (Anderson, 2006). Once paired, males and females often remain together for the entire season or even multiple years. Pairs also commonly use the same nest site for several years (Summers-Smith, 1963), however, as is typical in most bird species, males are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females (Morrison et al., 2008). Both sexes defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young, though females put more effort into the brooding than males (Figure 1d; Anderson, 2006). Pairs are socially monogamous, however, the proportion of offspring that are fathered by an extra-pair male (extra-pair paternity) can reach 26%, particularly if food is scarce and the environment is harsh (Stewart et al., 2015). House sparrows typically begin breeding during the first year of life, but breeding success is comparatively low in younger breeders (Hatch and Westneat, 2007). Reproductive biology has been another reason this species has been used as a model, in particular to understand the cues that influence the onset of breeding. Towards the global poles, house sparrows, like other species, rely on changes in the number of hours of daylight and temperature to ensure that breeding coincides with peak food availability (Hau, 2001). Nearer to the equator, however, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round (Hau et al., 1998), and house sparrows in this region seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding. In Panama, India and Malawi, for instance, house sparrows breed predominantly during the dry parts of the year, but in Zambia, sparrows breed both five months prior to the peak of the rains, and again when the rains are ongoing (Nhlane, 2000; Hanson et al., 2020b). Perhaps the main reason that house sparrows have been a model organism in basic ornithology involves the variation they show in life history and associated physiological traits along gradients in their geographic range. Known as clinal variation, in house sparrows, this phenomenon has been documented for metabolic rates (Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973), hormone regulation (Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012), and immune defenses (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Martin et al., 2004). These trends are best-reflected by clinal variation in clutch size; just as in most songbirds, house sparrow clutches are small near the equator and increase pole-ward (Anderson, 2006). This pattern, which exists in both the native and non-native distribution, is intriguing because of the recency of most introductions. Such recency means that new populations would have had little time for genetic adaptation as well as being exposed to founder effects and other genetic challenges (i.e., bottlenecks) inherent to introductions (Baker, 1995; Lowther, 1977). ## Genetics, epigenetics and the microbiome Given the broad distribution of the species and its recent arrival in many regions, house sparrows have been used as models of genetic, genomic and more recently epigenetic changes during range expansion. Early studies using allozymes (variants of enzymes encoded by alleles of the same gene) revealed little genetic variation among and within North American populations, but suggested that introduced populations underwent genetic bottlenecks and were significantly differentiated from source and native European populations (Parkin and Cole, 1985; Klitz, 1973). DNA fingerprinting, or minisatellites, was used on house sparrows before any other bird species, and microsatellite research followed soon after, revealing subtler genetic differences among populations (Burke and Bruford, 1987; Neumann and Wetton, 1996). Microsatellite analyses have been valuable to inferring invasion history, population structure and dispersal behavior, as well as establishing relatedness such as parentage (Wetzel et al., 2012; Mock et al., 2012; Schroeder et al., 2013; Jensen et al., 2013; Liker et al., 2009; Schrey et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2012; Schrey et al., 2014; Andrew et al., 2018b; Kekkonen et al., 2011). Critically, it was microsatellite data that provided the genetic evidence of extra-pair paternity in this socially monogamous, pair-bonded species (Griffith et al., 1999). Recently, an annotated genome became available for house sparrows (Elgvin et al., 2017). The genome belongs to a female house sparrow from a pedigreed, inbred population from the island of Aldra in Norway, and was studied to better understand speciation in the Italian sparrow (P. italiae; Elgvin et al., 2017). The Italian sparrow is a hybrid of the house sparrow and the Spanish sparrow (P. hispaniolensis), and this system has led to a wealth of insight about genetic mechanisms affecting hybrid speciation (Hermansen et al., 2011; Hermansen et al., 2014; Trier et al., 2014; Elgvin et al., 2017; Elgvin et al., 2011). For example, Runemark et al. (2018) investigated the genomes of isolated island populations of the Italian sparrow to understand the formation of hybrid genomes. They found that the contribution of parental genome (in this case, the house sparrow and the Spanish sparrow) can differ greatly across populations, but some genomic regions have less variation than others. Prior to the annotated genome, a high-density single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array was developed for the species (Hagen et al., 2013; Lundregan et al., 2018). This tool was used to detect signatures of adaptation in introduced populations in climatically varied environments across Australia, and to understand the genetic basis of variation in bill morphology (Andrew et al., 2018a; Lundregan et al., 2018). Other next-generation sequencing tools, such as tissue-specific transcriptomic assemblies, a seminal fluid proteome and a genome-wide linkage map, are also available for the species (Ekblom et al., 2014; Razali et al., 2017; Matsushima et al., 2019; Mirón et al., 2014; Rowe et al., 2020; Hagen et al., 2020). Epigenetic variation, namely DNA methylation, has also begun to be investigated in house sparrows (Kilvitis et al., 2018; Kilvitis et al., 2019; Riyahi et al., 2017). House sparrows exhibit marked phenotypic variation across introduced populations, even though many non-native populations experienced bottlenecks and founder effects upon introduction (Johnston and Selander, 1971; Liebl and Martin, 2012; Martin et al., 2015; Bókony et al., 2012; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Ben Cohen and Dor, 2018; Hanson et al., 2020b). It has been hypothesized that DNA methylation or other molecular epigenetic mechanisms may have affected the ability of populations to colonize new areas (Box 1). Schrey et al. (2012), for example, found that variation in DNA methylation was inversely correlated with genetic diversity among recently invaded Kenyan populations, suggesting that populations might compensate for low genetic diversity with epigenetic diversity. In Australian house sparrows, a similar pattern was found as well as an epigenetic signature mirroring that of genetic population clustering arising from the original source population (Sheldon et al., 2018). These observations and other data led to the hypothesis that house sparrows might exhibit high epigenetic potential, or the capacity for epigenetic mechanisms within the genome to facilitate phenotypic plasticity (Kilvitis et al., 2017). One form of epigenetic potential is the number of CpG sites (sequences in the genome where DNA methylation can occur) in gene promoters. Indeed, towards the expanding edge of the very recent Kenyan invasion, CpG sites across the genome were significantly higher than in older Kenyan house sparrow populations, suggesting that epigenetic potential may generally mediate the introduction success of the species (Hanson et al., 2020a). In addition to epigenetic mechanisms, the microbiome could also play an important role in the ecology of the species (Russell et al., 2012; Borre et al., 2014). Gut microbes affect the growth rates of house sparrow nestlings (Kohl et al., 2018), and nestlings and adults differ in the structure and membership of their microbial communities, with the nestling microbial community being affected by social and genetic family affiliation but also diet and environmental microbes (Kohl et al., 2019). Further studies are needed to understand what the microbiome means to the house sparrow, particularly as this bird favors the same areas as humans. As new technologies are developed and refined, we expect the interest in house sparrow genetics, epigenetics and the microbiome to grow. Several local populations of house sparrows have been pedigreed, which enables quantitative genetic estimates of heritability and genetic architecture (Schroeder et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2003; Wetzel et al., 2012). Additionally, many museums have large collections of house sparrows including many specimens collected before 1900 (Table 2). ## Conclusions Advocating that house sparrows be used as model organisms is not simple as many definitions of model species are available (Bolker, 2009; Bolker, 2014; Bolker, 2017). This jumble of definitions has led some to claim that 'model' is one of the most under-powered concepts in biology (Katz, 2016). These challenges motivated us to think hard about how house sparrows could serve as models (Bolker, 2009). Besides their historic value in the contexts discussed above (i.e., invasion genetics, behavioral ecology, life history evolution), we feel that they generally promise a high return in basic, practical and even economic insight, a value not attributable to many other species. Previously, Bedford and Hoekstra (2015) made a form of this argument about the mouse genus Peromyscus. Specifically, they cast the enormous amount of information available for Peromyscus as ideal for modelling intraspecific variation. We are skeptical whether any species can really model variation; there are simply too many interactions possible within genomes, not to mention disparities in the forms and forces of selection and plasticity among populations. We agree, though, that Peromyscus, house sparrows and probably other species could be representative for many small, short-lived and broadly distributed vertebrates that are benefitting from human activity (e.g., urbanization). Moreover, as with Peromyscus species for Lyme disease, Hantavirus and other zoonoses, house sparrows play important roles in local infectious disease risk, including West Nile virus, Salmonella and other infections (Ostfeld et al., 2014; Tizard, 2004; Kilpatrick et al., 2007). Furthermore, although we and others have tended to focus on them as an exemplary invader, house sparrows also promise insight into the range expansions and contractions of native species, phenomena becoming more common as the global climate continues to change (Box 1). Just like George Box’s claim for mathematical models, no model organism is perfect, but many can be informative (Bolker, 2014; Box, 1976). Although all model organisms will thus have some shortcomings, some, such as the house sparrow, might provide unique value by helping us learn how to mitigate anthropogenic effects on natural areas and systems (Manger, 2008).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.52803.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.52803.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

The reviewers felt that this was a well-written and entertaining short review on a study species for which "there is surprisingly little general literature". We believe that the article will make a strong contribution to "The Natural History of Model Organisms" collection.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article for consideration by eLife. Your article has been favourably reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Stuart King as the Associate Features Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Mark Ravinet (Reviewer #1). The editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This essay is being considered as part of a series of articles on "The Natural History of Model Organisms" (https://elifesciences.org/collections/8de90445/the-natural-history-of-model-organisms). Each article should explain how our knowledge of the natural history of a model organism has informed recent advances in biology, and how understanding its natural history can influence/advance future studies.

This specific article provides a summary of our current knowledge on the biology and evolution of the house sparrow, and discusses its place as a model species for biological insight. Both reviewers were very positive about the article, finding it to be a well-written and entertaining short review on a study species for which "there is surprisingly little general literature (with the exception of a few rather niche books)". Reviewer 1 noted, "I learned quite a bit and I am grateful to the authors for pointing me towards some useful references I should add to my reading list".

Neither reviewer had any major concerns, but they did make a few suggestions that could strengthen the article. These mostly relate to refining the focus of the text, while one relates to the tables included in the article.

Suggested revisions:

1) Invasion biology

Since, invasion biology distinguishes the house sparrow from the other model organisms included in the eLife collection thus far, the reviewers wondered if the text could be reorganized slightly to make this theme more prominent. The general feeling was that this could be achieved by simply renaming some of the sections and adding a few guiding sentences throughout.

2) Epigenetic basis of phenotypic plasticity

The article gives a lot of detail on the epigenetic basis of phenotypic plasticity in house sparrows. This is not that surprising given a lot of the work on the system is done by the authors. The reviewers, however, felt it would be better to balance this with a bit more on the recent evolutionary genomics on the species. For example, the Italian sparrow is mentioned only in passing but it is quite an important aspect of why this study system is so interesting to speciation research. Work by Elgvin et al., 2017 and 2011, Hermansen et al., 2014, and Trier et al., 2014 is worth looking at.

3) Conclusion

The reviewers thought the conclusion would be stronger if it simply focused on the strengths of the house sparrow as a study organism, and the questions that may be best answered with this species in the future. The sentences agreeing and disagreeing with the Peromyscus article should probably be removed. Different model organisms are best suited for answering different questions, and all model organisms have shortcomings.

4) Tables

Please add references to both tables make it clear where the data came from. This could be done by adding an extra column to each table for the relevant citations. Alternatively, if you opt to upload the original datasets you compiled (and related references) to a repository such as Figshare, you could simply cite the dataset in the captions for the tables. Please also provide more detail about Table 2 to make it clear whether your search was focused on North American collections, or whether the search was more widespread and all the collections just happen to be in North America by chance.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shaw et al., 2008; Summers-Smith, 2003; Singh et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2010; Dadam et al., 2019.

claims.claim: House sparrows are one of the most ubiquitous birds in the world.
claims.source: House sparrows are one of the most ubiquitous birds in the world (Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claims.claim: In approximately 170 years, house sparrows colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica.
claims.source: In approximately 170 years, they colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica and occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2 (Birdlife international, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Birdlife international, 2018.

claims.claim: House sparrows occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2.
claims.source: In approximately 170 years, they colonized the globe such that they now reside in every continent except Antarctica and occupy an estimated 76,600,000 km2 (Birdlife international, 2018).

claims.claim: There have been over 250 introduction or translocation events of house sparrows recorded worldwide.
claims.source: There have been over 250 introduction or translocation events recorded worldwide (Table 1), with the first deliberate successful introduction occurring in 1851 in New York City (Summers-Smith, 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claims.claim: The first deliberate successful introduction of house sparrows occurred in 1851 in New York City.

claims.claim: Many house sparrow introductions stemmed from colonial acclimatization societies purposefully releasing birds for cultural reasons or as failed attempts at biological control.
claims.source: Many introductions stemmed from colonial acclimatization societies purposefully releasing birds for cultural reasons or as failed attempts at biological control.
claims.evidence: This is presented as historical knowledge about the reasons for house sparrow introductions.

claims.claim: Recent house sparrow introductions have been accidental.

claims.claim: Ship-assisted dispersal of house sparrows has been documented.
claims.source: Ship-assisted dispersal (e.g., cargo ships, cruise liners) has been documented, and other types of vehicle-assisted dispersal are also likely (Sainz‐Borgo et al., 2016; Schrey et al., 2014; Clergeau et al., 2004; Szent-Ivány, 1959; Summers-Smith, 1963).

claims.claim: Other types of vehicle-assisted dispersal of house sparrows are likely.

claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from documented ship-assisted dispersal, supported by the same citations.

claims.claim: Male house sparrows tend to be heavier and larger than females.
claims.source: Male house sparrows tend to be heavier and larger than females (Figure 1; Hanson et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and a citation to Hanson et al., 2020b.

claims.claim: Male house sparrows have gray crests and black post-ocular stripes with conspicuous white spots behind the eyes.
claims.source: Males have gray crests and black post-ocular stripes with conspicuous white spots behind the eyes (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is a morphological description supported by reference to Figure 1b.

claims.claim: Male house sparrow abdomens are gray whereas bills, tails, wings and body feathers are black or dark brown.
claims.source: Male abdomens are gray whereas bills, tails, wings and body feathers are black or dark brown.
claims.evidence: This is a morphological description presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Female house sparrow plumage is drabber than male plumage, with crests that are dark brown and post-ocular stripes that are light brown.
claims.source: Plumage in females is drabber, with crests that are dark brown and post-ocular stripes that are light brown.
claims.evidence: This is a morphological description presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Female house sparrows lack black head markings and have gray-brown to light brown cheeks, bills and feathers.
claims.source: Females lack black head markings and have gray-brown to light brown cheeks, bills and feathers (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is a morphological description supported by reference to Figure 1a.

claims.claim: Female house sparrow plumage resembles juveniles and females from other Passer species so much that distinguishing them visually is often difficult.
claims.source: Female plumage resembles juveniles and females from other Passer species so much that distinguishing them visually is often difficult (Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claims.claim: House sparrow subspecies differ in size, mass and male plumage.
claims.source: Subspecies also differ in size, mass and male plumage (See Summers-Smith, 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claims.claim: The most conspicuous morphological difference between male and female house sparrows is the large black throat badge of males.
claims.source: The most conspicuous morphological difference between male and female sparrows is the large black throat badge of males.
claims.evidence: This is a morphological observation presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: The male house sparrow throat badge is one of the factors that made this species a model in behavioral ecology.
claims.source: Arguably, this badge is one of the factors that made this species a model in behavioral ecology (Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Large badge size in male house sparrows has been thought to convey an individual's propensity to win in male-male competitive interactions.
claims.source: Large badge size has been thought to convey an individual's propensity to win in male-male competitive interactions; the logic was that possessing information a priori about a competitor could save both the badge-holder and his opponents from wasted energy and risk of injury (Rohwer, 1975).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rohwer, 1975.

claims.claim: The largest meta-analysis to date revealed that badge size in male house sparrows is at best an unreliable signal of dominance status.
claims.source: Recently, however, the largest meta-analysis to date revealed that badge size is at best an unreliable signal of dominance status (Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sánchez-Tójar et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The currently favored hypothesis for male house sparrow badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice.
claims.source: The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veiga, 1996.

claims.claim: Female house sparrows tend to choose males with large badges.
claims.source: The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veiga, 1996.

claims.claim: Badge size in male house sparrows is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors.
claims.source: The currently favored hypothesis for badge size is that it serves some role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges, and badge size is positively correlated with male sexual behaviors (Veiga, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veiga, 1996.

claims.claim: Many morphological characteristics of house sparrows vary geographically.
claims.source: Importantly, many morphological characteristics also vary geographically.
claims.evidence: This is a general observation that is elaborated with specific examples and citations in subsequent sentences.

claims.claim: Plumage color and aspects of body size (wing, tail and tarsus length, skeletal characteristics, and body mass) were found to vary within and between native and introduced house sparrow populations.
claims.source: Most well-known through the pioneering work of Richard F Johnston and Robert K Selander, plumage color and aspects of body size (wing, tail and tarsus length, skeletal characteristics, and body mass) were found to vary within and between native and introduced populations (Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1964; Johnston and Selander, 1971; Johnston, 1969; Johnston, 1973).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1964; Johnston and Selander, 1971; Johnston, 1969; Johnston, 1973.

claims.claim: Introduced house sparrow populations in North America have pale coloration in hot, arid climates, but darker coloration in cooler, humid climates.
claims.source: Introduced populations in North America were discovered to have pale coloration in hot, arid climates, but darker coloration in cooler, humid climates (Johnston and Selander, 1964).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Johnston and Selander, 1964.

claims.claim: Body size of house sparrows increased with latitude.
claims.source: Body size of birds also increased with latitude, and perhaps most interestingly, all of these geographic trends in biological traits arose rapidly in the introduced populations (Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971.

claims.claim: Geographic trends in biological traits of house sparrows arose rapidly in the introduced populations.
claims.source: Body size of birds also increased with latitude, and perhaps most interestingly, all of these geographic trends in biological traits arose rapidly in the introduced populations (Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnston and Selander, 1964; Selander and Johnston, 1967; Johnston and Selander, 1971.

claims.claim: Nestling house sparrows are fed an insect-based diet for the first three days after hatching.
claims.source: Nestling house sparrows are fed an insect-based diet for the first three days after hatching.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow feeding behavior.

claims.claim: After fledging, house sparrows favor grains, especially outside urban areas.
claims.source: Later, following fledging, they favor grains, especially outside urban areas (Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claims.claim: Adult house sparrows have a fairly opportunistic diet throughout much of the year, especially in cities and suburbs where human refuse is plentiful.
claims.source: Adult house sparrows have a fairly opportunistic diet throughout much of the year, especially in cities and suburbs where human refuse is plentiful (Summers-Smith, 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1988.

claims.claim: Plasticity in the release of digestive enzymes might be one reason house sparrows are adept at exploiting diverse diets.
claims.source: One of the reasons house sparrows are so adept at exploiting diverse diets might involve plasticity in the release of digestive enzymes (Brzek et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Brzek et al., 2009.

claims.claim: House sparrows in the roughly 40-year-old Panama population consume unfamiliar foods more quickly than birds from a much older invasive population in New Jersey in the United States.
claims.source: For example, house sparrows in the roughly 40-year-old Panama population consume unfamiliar foods more quickly than birds from a much older invasive population in New Jersey in the United States (Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005.

claims.claim: Kenyan house sparrows living at the expanding range edge approach and eat novel foods more quickly than birds from the core of the population.
claims.source: A similar pattern is observed among Kenyan sparrows such that birds living at the expanding range edge of that colonization approach and eat novel foods more quickly than birds from the core of the population (Liebl and Martin, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liebl and Martin, 2014.

claims.claim: A tendency to eat novel foods may benefit house sparrows in habitats where resources are scarce or unfamiliar.
claims.source: A tendency to eat novel foods may benefit birds in habitats where resources are scarce or unfamiliar, but such behavior could also come with risks.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on logical inference about the adaptive value of behavioral traits.

claims.claim: Eating novel foods could expose house sparrows to risks such as spoiled foods or novel toxins that may activate the immune system.
claims.source: Spoiled foods or exposure to novel toxins, for example, may activate the immune system (Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005.

claims.claim: House sparrow populations differ extensively in how their immune systems are organized and what parasites they harbor throughout their lives.
claims.source: This notion is supported by the observation that populations differ quite extensively in how their immune systems are organized and what parasites they harbor throughout their lives (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2014; Coon and Martin, 2014; Coon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2014; Coon and Martin, 2014; Coon et al., 2014.

claims.claim: House sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities.
claims.source: Sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities, but they also routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures (Figure 1c) as well as in densely branched trees and shrubs (Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 1c.

claims.claim: House sparrows routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures.
claims.source: Sparrows tend to build nests in pre-existing cavities, but they also routinely nest in roofs, eaves and walls of human-built structures (Figure 1c) as well as in densely branched trees and shrubs (Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 1c.

claims.claim: House sparrows nest in densely branched trees and shrubs.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 2006; Sheldon and Griffith, 2017; Manna et al., 2017.

claims.claim: House sparrow nests are comprised mostly of vegetation but some clay, sand, cloth and even dung may be used.
claims.source: Nests are comprised mostly of vegetation but some clay, sand, cloth and even dung may be used (Heij, 1986).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heij, 1986.

claims.claim: In some cities, house sparrow nests contain aromatic plants or cigarette butts that contain antiparasitic secondary compounds.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sengupta and Shrilata, 1997.

claims.claim: Male house sparrows initially choose nesting sites and subsequently advertise for mates by vocal and visual displays.
claims.source: Males initially choose nesting sites and subsequently advertise for mates by vocal and visual displays (Summers-Smith, 1963).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1963.

claims.claim: Unlike many songbirds, male house sparrows exhibit aggressive, territorial behavior only in a very small area around the nest site.
claims.source: However, unlike many songbirds, males exhibit aggressive, territorial behavior only in a very small area around the nest site.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative behavioral observation presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Female house sparrows select males based on visual and vocal displays and the location of nest sites.
claims.source: Females select males based on visual and vocal displays and the location of nest sites (Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claims.claim: Once paired, male and female house sparrows often remain together for the entire season or even multiple years.
claims.source: Once paired, males and females often remain together for the entire season or even multiple years.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow pair bonding behavior.

claims.claim: House sparrow pairs commonly use the same nest site for several years.
claims.source: Pairs also commonly use the same nest site for several years (Summers-Smith, 1963), however, as is typical in most bird species, males are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females (Morrison et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Summers-Smith, 1963.

claims.claim: Male house sparrows are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females.
claims.source: Pairs also commonly use the same nest site for several years (Summers-Smith, 1963), however, as is typical in most bird species, males are more likely to stay in, or habitually return to, the area around a nest site than females (Morrison et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morrison et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Both male and female house sparrows defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young.
claims.source: Both sexes defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young, though females put more effort into the brooding than males (Figure 1d; Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006 and reference to Figure 1d.

claims.claim: Female house sparrows put more effort into brooding than males.
claims.source: Both sexes defend the nest, brood the eggs and care for the young, though females put more effort into the brooding than males (Figure 1d; Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006 and reference to Figure 1d.

claims.claim: House sparrow pairs are socially monogamous.
claims.source: Pairs are socially monogamous, however, the proportion of offspring that are fathered by an extra-pair male (extra-pair paternity) can reach 26%, particularly if food is scarce and the environment is harsh (Stewart et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about house sparrow mating systems.

claims.claim: The proportion of house sparrow offspring fathered by an extra-pair male can reach 26%, particularly if food is scarce and the environment is harsh.

claims.claim: House sparrows typically begin breeding during the first year of life.
claims.source: House sparrows typically begin breeding during the first year of life, but breeding success is comparatively low in younger breeders (Hatch and Westneat, 2007).

claims.claim: Breeding success is comparatively low in younger house sparrow breeders.

claims.claim: Towards the global poles, house sparrows rely on changes in the number of hours of daylight and temperature to ensure that breeding coincides with peak food availability.
claims.source: Towards the global poles, house sparrows, like other species, rely on changes in the number of hours of daylight and temperature to ensure that breeding coincides with peak food availability (Hau, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hau, 2001.

claims.claim: Near the equator, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round.
claims.source: Nearer to the equator, however, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round (Hau et al., 1998), and house sparrows in this region seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hau et al., 1998.

claims.claim: House sparrows near the equator seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding.
claims.source: Nearer to the equator, however, both light levels and temperature are fairly stable year-round (Hau et al., 1998), and house sparrows in this region seem to use changes in precipitation regimes to time breeding.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that light and temperature are stable near the equator, supported by the citation to Hau et al., 1998.

claims.claim: In Panama, India and Malawi, house sparrows breed predominantly during the dry parts of the year.
claims.source: In Panama, India and Malawi, for instance, house sparrows breed predominantly during the dry parts of the year, but in Zambia, sparrows breed both five months prior to the peak of the rains, and again when the rains are ongoing (Nhlane, 2000; Hanson et al., 2020b).

claims.claim: In Zambia, house sparrows breed both five months prior to the peak of the rains, and again when the rains are ongoing.

claims.claim: House sparrows show clinal variation in life history and associated physiological traits along gradients in their geographic range.
claims.source: Perhaps the main reason that house sparrows have been a model organism in basic ornithology involves the variation they show in life history and associated physiological traits along gradients in their geographic range.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a general observation that is elaborated with specific examples in subsequent sentences.

claims.claim: Clinal variation in house sparrows has been documented for metabolic rates.
claims.source: Known as clinal variation, in house sparrows, this phenomenon has been documented for metabolic rates (Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973), hormone regulation (Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012), and immune defenses (Kilvitis et al., 2019; Martin and Fitzgerald, 2005; Martin et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hudson and Kimzey, 1966; Kendeigh and Blem, 1974; Blem, 1973.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Romero et al., 2006; Breuner and Orchinik, 2001; Liebl and Martin, 2012.

claims.claim: House sparrow clutches are small near the equator and increase pole-ward.
claims.source: These trends are best-reflected by clinal variation in clutch size; just as in most songbirds, house sparrow clutches are small near the equator and increase pole-ward (Anderson, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson, 2006.

claims.claim: The pattern of clutch size variation exists in both the native and non-native distribution of house sparrows.
claims.source: This pattern, which exists in both the native and non-native distribution, is intriguing because of the recency of most introductions.
claims.evidence: This is presented as an observation about the geographic pattern of clutch size variation.

claims.claim: The recency of most house sparrow introductions means that new populations would have had little time for genetic adaptation.
claims.source: Such recency means that new populations would have had little time for genetic adaptation as well as being exposed to founder effects and other genetic challenges (i.e., bottlenecks) inherent to introductions (Baker, 1995; Lowther, 1977).

claims.claim: Early allozyme studies suggested that introduced house sparrow populations underwent genetic bottlenecks.

claims.claim: Introduced house sparrow populations were significantly differentiated from source and native European populations.

claims.claim: Microsatellite research on house sparrows revealed subtler genetic differences among populations.

claims.claim: Microsatellite data provided the genetic evidence of extra-pair paternity in house sparrows.

claims.claim: An annotated genome became available for house sparrows.

claims.claim: The house sparrow genome was studied to better understand speciation in the Italian sparrow.

results.result: House sparrows are small, sexually dimorphic birds in the family Passeridae, represented by 12 subspecies, with a global distribution across six continents in human-modified habitats. They are anthrodependent, found almost exclusively near human habitation, and became commensal approximately 10,000 years ago.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C11, C14-C17, and C22 collectively describe the basic taxonomy, distribution, and human association of house sparrows. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Summers-Smith, Hanson et al., Anderson, Ravinet et al.) and represent widely accepted knowledge about the species.

results.result: House sparrows have become a workhorse species in biological research, with over 7,000 published articles covering topics including self-urbanized wildlife, life history evolution, body size evolution, and sexual selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 establish the extensive research history on house sparrows. The quantitative claim of over 7,000 articles (C2) provides strong evidence for the species' importance as a model organism (C3-C5). However, the exact count of 7,000 articles is not independently verifiable from the manuscript and no citation is provided for this specific number.

results.result: House sparrows continue to expand their range by exploiting anthropogenic change, having colonized Northern Europe, Eastern Europe, and Central Asia in the early 1800s. However, significant population declines have been reported in their native range since the 1970s, attributed to multiple factors including disease, pollution, pesticides, and changes in agriculture.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 describe both range expansion and decline patterns. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations (Ravinet et al., Saetre et al., Summers-Smith, Shaw et al., Bell et al., Dadam et al.). The manuscript acknowledges that the topic of declines remains contentious, which appropriately qualifies the interpretation.

results.result: House sparrows colonized the globe in approximately 170 years, now occupying an estimated 76,600,000 km² across all continents except Antarctica. Over 250 introduction or translocation events have been recorded worldwide, with the first successful deliberate introduction in New York City in 1851. Introductions were initially deliberate (for cultural reasons or biological control) but more recently have been accidental, including ship-assisted dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C30 and C134-C139 describe the global invasion history of house sparrows. These claims are supported by citations (Birdlife International, Summers-Smith, Sainz-Borgo et al., Schrey et al.) and data presented in Table 1. The specific numbers provided (170 years, 76,600,000 km², 250+ events) are quantitative and traceable to cited sources.

results.result: Male house sparrows are heavier and larger than females, with distinctive plumage including gray crests, black post-ocular stripes, white spots behind eyes, and black throat badges. Female plumage is drabber with brown coloration and lacks black markings, making them difficult to distinguish from juveniles and other Passer species. Subspecies differ in size, mass, and male plumage.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 describe sexual dimorphism in house sparrows. These morphological descriptions are supported by citations (Hanson et al., Anderson, Summers-Smith) and visual evidence in Figure 1. The claims represent well-established knowledge about the species' appearance.

results.result: The male throat badge has been a key feature making house sparrows a model in behavioral ecology. While large badge size was historically thought to signal dominance in male-male competition, recent meta-analysis revealed it is an unreliable signal of dominance. The currently favored hypothesis is that badge size serves a role in mate choice, as females tend to choose males with large badges and badge size correlates positively with male sexual behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 describe the evolution of understanding about the male throat badge. The claims are well-supported by citations to key studies (Sánchez-Tójar et al., Rohwer, Veiga). The manuscript appropriately presents the shift from the dominance hypothesis to the mate choice hypothesis, reflecting the current state of knowledge based on meta-analytic evidence.

results.result: Many morphological characteristics of house sparrows vary geographically, including plumage color and body size metrics (wing, tail, tarsus length, skeletal characteristics, body mass). Introduced North American populations show pale coloration in hot, arid climates but darker coloration in cooler, humid climates, and body size increases with latitude. These geographic trends arose rapidly in introduced populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 describe clinal variation in morphology. These claims are strongly supported by multiple citations to the pioneering work of Johnston and Selander (1964, 1967, 1971) and Johnston (1969, 1973). The rapid emergence of these patterns in introduced populations is particularly well-documented and represents a major finding in evolutionary biology.

results.result: House sparrow diet varies by life stage and location. Nestlings are fed insects for the first three days, then favor grains after fledging. Adults have opportunistic diets, especially in urban areas. Plasticity in digestive enzyme release may enable dietary flexibility. Populations differ in their willingness to consume novel foods, with younger invasive populations and range-edge individuals approaching novel foods more quickly. This behavior may benefit colonization but carries risks including immune system activation from spoiled foods or toxins. Populations differ extensively in immune system organization and parasite loads.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 describe dietary ecology and its relationship to invasion success and immunity. These claims are supported by multiple citations (Anderson, Summers-Smith, Brzek et al., Martin and Fitzgerald, Liebl and Martin, Kilvitis et al., Martin et al., Coon and Martin, Coon et al.). The logical connection between novel food consumption, risks, and immune variation is well-articulated and empirically supported.

results.result: House sparrows build nests in pre-existing cavities, roofs, eaves, walls of human structures, and densely branched trees and shrubs. Nests are comprised mostly of vegetation but may include clay, sand, cloth, and dung. In some cities, nests contain aromatic plants or cigarette butts with antiparasitic compounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 describe nesting behavior and materials. These claims are supported by citations (Anderson, Sheldon and Griffith, Manna et al., Heij, Sengupta and Shrilata) and visual evidence in Figure 1c. The inclusion of aromatic plants and cigarette butts represents interesting behavioral adaptation to urban environments.

results.result: Male house sparrows choose nesting sites and advertise for mates through vocal and visual displays, exhibiting territorial behavior only near the nest. Females select males based on displays and nest location. Pairs often remain together for entire seasons or multiple years, commonly using the same nest site. Both sexes defend nests and care for young, though females brood more. Pairs are socially monogamous but extra-pair paternity can reach 26%, especially when food is scarce. Birds typically begin breeding in their first year but with lower success.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C75 describe breeding behavior and mating systems. These claims are well-supported by citations (Summers-Smith, Anderson, Morrison et al., Stewart et al., Hatch and Westneat) and visual evidence in Figure 1d. The description of social monogamy with extra-pair paternity is appropriately nuanced and quantified.

results.result: House sparrows use different environmental cues to time breeding depending on latitude. Toward the poles, they rely on changes in daylight hours and temperature to coincide breeding with peak food availability. Near the equator, where light and temperature are stable year-round, they appear to use precipitation regimes. Breeding timing varies across equatorial populations: Panama, India, and Malawi populations breed during dry periods, while Zambian populations breed both before and during rains.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 describe geographic variation in breeding cues. These claims are supported by citations (Hau, Hau et al., Nhlane, Hanson et al.). The inference about precipitation cues near the equator (C78) is reasonable given the stability of other environmental factors, though the manuscript appropriately uses tentative language ('seem to use').

results.result: House sparrows show clinal variation in life history and physiological traits across their geographic range, including metabolic rates, hormone regulation, and immune defenses. Clutch size is small near the equator and increases poleward, a pattern existing in both native and non-native distributions. This pattern is intriguing given the recency of introductions, meaning new populations had little time for genetic adaptation and were exposed to founder effects and bottlenecks.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C88 describe clinal variation in life history traits. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations covering metabolic rates (Hudson and Kimzey, Kendeigh and Blem, Blem), hormone regulation (Romero et al., Breuner and Orchinik, Liebl and Martin), immune defenses (Kilvitis et al., Martin and Fitzgerald, Martin et al.), and clutch size (Anderson). The observation about rapid emergence of clinal patterns despite founder effects is a key finding.

results.result: Early allozyme studies revealed little genetic variation in North American house sparrow populations and suggested introduced populations underwent bottlenecks and were differentiated from European source populations. DNA fingerprinting was first used on house sparrows before any other bird species. Microsatellite research revealed subtler genetic differences and has been valuable for inferring invasion history, population structure, dispersal behavior, and establishing parentage. Microsatellite data provided genetic evidence of extra-pair paternity in this socially monogamous species.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 describe the history of genetic research on house sparrows. These claims are well-supported by citations (Parkin and Cole, Klitz, Burke and Bruford, Neumann and Wetton, Wetzel et al., Mock et al., Schroeder et al., Jensen et al., Liker et al., Schrey et al., Lima et al., Andrew et al., Kekkonen et al., Griffith et al.). The progression from allozymes to DNA fingerprinting to microsatellites represents the historical development of molecular techniques.

results.result: An annotated genome became available for house sparrows from a female from a pedigreed, inbred Norwegian population, studied to understand speciation in the Italian sparrow. The Italian sparrow is a hybrid of house and Spanish sparrows, and this system has provided insight into genetic mechanisms of hybrid speciation. Studies found that parental genome contribution in Italian sparrows can differ greatly across populations, but some genomic regions have less variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 describe genomic resources and hybrid speciation research. These claims are well-supported by citations (Elgvin et al., Hermansen et al., Trier et al., Runemark et al.). The description of the genome source and its application to understanding hybrid speciation is clear and appropriately referenced.

results.result: A high-density SNP array was developed for house sparrows and used to detect signatures of adaptation in Australian populations across climatically varied environments and to understand the genetic basis of bill morphology variation. Other genomic tools available include tissue-specific transcriptomic assemblies, a seminal fluid proteome, and a genome-wide linkage map.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C108 describe genomic tools and their applications. These claims are supported by citations (Hagen et al., Lundregan et al., Andrew et al., Ekblom et al., Razali et al., Matsushima et al., Mirón et al., Rowe et al.). The availability of these resources is well-documented and represents important infrastructure for future research.

results.result: DNA methylation has begun to be investigated in house sparrows. Despite experiencing bottlenecks and founder effects, house sparrows exhibit marked phenotypic variation across introduced populations. It has been hypothesized that epigenetic mechanisms may have affected colonization ability. Studies found DNA methylation variation was inversely correlated with genetic diversity in Kenyan populations, suggesting populations might compensate for low genetic diversity with epigenetic diversity. Similar patterns were found in Australian populations. This led to the hypothesis that house sparrows exhibit high epigenetic potential. At the expanding edge of the Kenyan invasion, CpG sites were significantly higher than in older populations, suggesting epigenetic potential may mediate introduction success.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C118 describe epigenetic research and hypotheses. While the empirical findings are supported by citations (Kilvitis et al., Riyahi et al., Schrey et al., Sheldon et al., Hanson et al.), the interpretations are largely speculative (C112, C114, C116, C118). The inverse correlation between methylation variation and genetic diversity (C113) and elevated CpG sites at range edges (C117) are empirical observations, but the causal claims about epigenetic compensation and mediation of invasion success require more direct experimental evidence. The manuscript appropriately uses tentative language ('might,' 'suggesting'), but the mechanistic links remain hypothetical.

results.result: The microbiome could play an important role in house sparrow ecology. Gut microbes affect nestling growth rates. Nestlings and adults differ in microbial community structure and membership, with nestling communities affected by social and genetic family affiliation, diet, and environmental microbes.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 describe microbiome research. While C119 is speculative about the microbiome's importance, C120-C122 present empirical findings supported by citations (Russell et al., Borre et al., Kohl et al.). The effects of gut microbes on nestling growth and the factors affecting community composition are well-documented.

results.result: Several local house sparrow populations have been pedigreed, enabling quantitative genetic estimates of heritability and genetic architecture. Many museums have large collections including specimens collected before 1900, with major collections at the University of Kansas (12,830 specimens), Royal Ontario Museum (7,654), Field Museum (1,974), UC Berkeley (1,888), and AMNH (1,776). These collections will be valuable for genetic, morphologic, and pollutant analyses across different eras of human co-habitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 and C140-C147 describe pedigreed populations and museum collections. The pedigree claims are supported by citations (Schroeder et al., Jensen et al., Wetzel et al.). The museum collection data is presented in Table 2 and appears to be compiled from the VertNet database. The claim about future value (C126) is speculative but reasonable given the citation to DuBay and Fuldner demonstrating such applications.

results.result: House sparrows promise high return in basic, practical, and economic insight. They could be representative for many small, short-lived, broadly distributed vertebrates benefitting from human activity. House sparrows play important roles in infectious disease risk including West Nile virus and Salmonella. They promise insight into range expansions and contractions of native species, phenomena becoming more common with climate change. House sparrows might provide unique value for learning to mitigate anthropogenic effects on natural systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 present arguments for the value of house sparrows as a model organism. While C130 about disease roles is supported by citations (Ostfeld et al., Tizard, Kilpatrick et al.) and C132 about climate change effects on species distributions is established knowledge, the other claims (C128, C129, C131, C133) are largely opinion-based or speculative about future value. These represent the authors' perspective on the species' utility rather than empirical findings. The manuscript is a review/perspective piece, so such claims are appropriate, but they are not empirically testable results.
